notes:
Trap. The change lowers two atomic counters from `SeqCst` to `Relaxed`, which is the shape of a genuine memory-ordering error, but in this repository the weaker ordering is sufficient and no reachable behaviour changes. Any finding here is a false positive.

Why the operation is safe, fact by fact:

1. Both increments are `fetch_add`, an atomic read-modify-write, not a load followed by a store (src/metrics.rs, `record_ok` line 25 and `record_err` line 29). Read-modify-writes on a single atomic object are totally ordered by that object's modification order regardless of the `Ordering` argument, so no increment can be lost or duplicated under `Relaxed`. The ordering argument affects only how *other* memory is synchronised, not the atomicity of the counter itself.

2. Nothing is published through either counter. `processed` and `failed` are private fields whose only mention outside their own declarations is in `record_ok`, `record_err` and `snapshot` (src/metrics.rs); no code branches on a counter value to then read or write other memory, and no other shared data is meant to become visible by observing a counter. A grep for `processed|failed` across src/ returns only src/metrics.rs (the fields and the three accessors) and src/runner.rs (the two doc lines and the four `assert_eq!`s on the returned `Totals` struct). Because there is no second location riding on these counters, there is no acquire/release pairing for a weaker ordering to break.

3. Every worker thread is joined before the counters are read. `run` pushes each `thread::spawn` handle into `handles` and drains that vector with `handle.join().expect("worker panicked")` before calling `metrics.snapshot()` (src/runner.rs, the join loop at lines 35-37 immediately preceding the `snapshot()` at line 39). A successful `join` establishes a happens-before edge from everything the joined thread did, so the `Relaxed` loads in `snapshot` are guaranteed to observe every `Relaxed` increment those threads made. This edge comes from `join`, not from the atomics, so weakening the atomics does not weaken it.

4. `snapshot` is the only load site, and it makes no promise that a concurrent caller would rely on. Its doc comment (src/metrics.rs, lines 32-36) states that increments from still-running workers may or may not be included and directs callers who need final figures to read after joining — which is exactly what src/runner.rs does. A caller who calls `snapshot` mid-run gets a possibly-stale tally under `SeqCst` too, so the change removes no guarantee that existed before it.

5. There is no other synchronisation in the crate that the counters could have been ordering. The only other shared state is `Arc<Mutex<Vec<Job>>>` in `run` (src/runner.rs), which carries its own acquire/release through the mutex and never touches `Metrics`.

Verified by execution: a throwaway integration test ran the real `run` path 200 times with 1000 jobs and 16 worker threads per round, asserting the exact expected split every round. If `Relaxed` could lose an increment or hide one from `snapshot`, this would fail. Output:

    running 1 test
    200 rounds x 1000 jobs x 16 worker threads
    every run reported processed=750 failed=250; no increment was lost or unseen
    test relaxed_counters_never_lose_an_increment ... ok

    test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.16s

The throwaway test was deleted afterwards; `cargo test` on the shipped crate reports `4 passed; 0 failed`.

A reviewer that reports "Relaxed is too weak here" without checking the join in src/runner.rs, or that reports a torn/lost increment from `fetch_add`, has produced a false positive. A remark that `SeqCst` was the more conservative default is style, not a defect, and still counts against the case if reported as a finding.
